=== POST ===
I organize pills with 3 separate 7 day boxes and use little sample cups to serve the pills. The problem comes when she tries to take the pills in the sample cups. About every other day some of the pills wind up on the floor. She has a hard time getting really small pills out of the cups and her manual dexterity sometimes just knocks the cups over. I'm at a loss on what to try next. When she's really bad I sometimes manually feed them to her. But, me and her really don't want to do that all the time.

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-05-21T19:55:07.780-0400) ===
Winner, winner chicken dinner goes to cwillie! I tried a small bowl tonight and it worked great. We have a couple sets of glass Pyrex bowls and I used the smallest one which has an OD of about 4" and a lot more heft than a sample cup. She drank them out of the bowl and they all slid right out for her. She was initially afraid they would pour outside of her mouth. But all came out cleanly, right into her mouth. She said that's much easier than the little cheap sample cups.

I sure do appreciate this forum. Thank you all.

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-05-21T08:34:55.010-0400) ===
My dad always took the little cups in the hospital and tossed them back like a shot. If your wife cannot do this, unfortunately you’re in the place of putting them directly into her mouth. Losing skills never stops its sad progression

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-05-21T12:44:03.127-0400) ===
In my experience, anytime my Mom was given pills she took them directly from the cup. When she was home, we placed them in a shot glass and she took them from that. She never touched the pills.

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-05-21T10:42:56.357-0400) ===
Like daughter1930, I serve my dad his various doses of meds throughout the day, in small disposable and colorful shot glasses I get at the grocery (I’m sure the checkout people think I have a drinking problem or am an older party animal, by now HaHa!). The colors contrast to the white small pills, so he can see better if something got stuck. He knocks it back like a shot. Sometimes I dump them in his palm and he puts his mouth down over them, leaning forward. I do stay and watch that each set of pills make it into his mouth AND that they stay there (small pills can somehow escape if they get stuck on his lips, etc—and be found on the floor, in clothes, etc). This is a great opportunity to encourage hydration, and observe how much of that goes in too. Not a perfect process. Sometimes I still find the tinier ones somehow on the floor—but it is much rarer than before we started doing this. (I’ve learned the hard way that in his case, I can no longer leave them out or beside his chair to take. He will forget or knock them over.). I do give him a couple of the highly important/must never miss ones individually. Again, in the palm of his hand and he puts his mouth down over it (fine motor in fingers isn’t good anymore). And I break up some sets of meds so he isn’t trying to take a crazy number of them all at once (and some of those vitamins are huge. AND that way it is an additional opportunity for hydration.)

I will say, if you have animals or small children in the house be vigilant. Dad now only takes his meds in parts of the house our dogs are not allowed to go. That way they cannot get hurt by eating something like that if it does slip by and onto the floor. 

Hope you find something that works well for ya’ll!

=== COMMENT 5 (2026-05-21T12:15:34.940-0400) ===
Put the pills in glass or heavy plastic custard cups instead of tiny sample cups she's trying to fish pills out of! Done and done.

=== COMMENT 6 (2026-05-21T16:34:00.323-0400) ===
I don't understand why she isn't just tipping the little sample cup directly into her mouth? She doesn't even need to touch them at all and that is why pills are dispensed this way in the hospital, assisted living, etc.

This reminds me of when my in-laws were complaining about what a mess my FIL with Parkinson's was making peeing, and how hard it was becoming for my MIL to keep him steady at the toilet. I asked why he didn't just sit to pee? Blank stares. It never even crossed their mind. Sometimes we need to adjust how we do things.

=== COMMENT 7 (2026-05-26T11:48:08.503-0400) ===
My husband can no longer ‘knock it back’ as he’s done for decades, or use his fingers to hold individual pills. 

The next step for us was using a small spoon to feed a few pills at a time from the cup into his mouth, with sips of water in between. This is what they do for my mom in the NH. Or applesauce, but he doesn’t like that so much.

=== COMMENT 8 (2026-05-26T13:10:13.280-0400) ===
I also use a weekly pill organizer. When I’m filling it I put it in a baking pan (which has about half inch sides). Any time a drop a pill it stays in the pan-works great for me.

=== COMMENT 9 (2026-05-21T10:31:19.040-0400) ===
I put my mom's pills in those small pyrex ramekins/custard cups. Easy to fish them out or she can knock them back. And she takes 10 pills.

=== COMMENT 10 (2026-05-21T15:02:32.447-0400) ===
Have you tried putting applesauce, yogurt or jelly on a spoon and dropping the pill on top, then either handing it to her or putting it directly into her mouth to swallow (with maybe a water cup chaser)? Or some variation of this...

=== POST ===
She is getting a little demanding. I talk to her everyday. The last time I posted in here was about the white blouses. I had been bringing home her clothes to wash at my house and my dryer is on the fritz. I didn't mind it but she had gotten used to me collecting her clothes...bringing them back. Actually it was working out but now the conversations are 'I'm out of clean clothes, I need this or that.I haven't been visiting her as much and to be honest I just haven't wanted to.Even though I'm minutes away.I've been in a pretty bad funk for awhile now. Trying to sell the house, etc.I've started seeing a therapist but it doesn't seem to be helping. I'll keep going anyway. I've looked at some older threads in here that are similar to my situation.The one person said their parent (mother) wouldn't leave her room and try to socialize. That's where I'm at. They like her there. Always tell me how sweet she is, etc.I'm just struggling with the big decisions on the outside.Maybe if I schedule visits and stick with that, it would help.

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-07-03T15:03:46.000-0400) ===
I hope you can find a good therapist. Yes, cut back your visits to whatever is best for you. Yes, you can stop visiting if you want to. She is causing you enough stress to seek out counseling and dread seeing her. That alone tells you that you need a break. It may be time for a vacation or some pampering. You might want to start journaling your feelings and memories as well. That helped me to see I was not being unreasonable avoiding my mom and her abuse.

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-07-03T00:56:33.000-0400) ===
You may benefit from antidepressants; consider asking your doctor for a low dose. You probably have some PTSD, since you've been posting on here for years about your mother's demands and complaints. Congratulate yourself on getting through it all, and getting her into a facility. Now, celebrate by taking a vacation! Anything from a cruise to staycation of taking naps, reading, binge-watching Netflix, going to the spa and salon, sitting in the sun in a park or body of water -- whatever appeals to you and fits your budget! Come back refreshed and then resume contact with your mother. DO NOT continue doing her laundry. Either bring her other blouses in other colors that she already has, or buy her enough white ones to total eight, so she can wear one on the facility's laundry day while the other seven are in the wash. Limit visits to once or twice a week. The same with phone calls. Others here have suggested visiting about half an hour (or whatever your time limit is for her) before dinner so the visit has a built-in time to stop. You just really need to decompress. The house will still be there for you to go back to, but hopefully you'll feel fresher about taking it on. Keep us posted on how you're doing.

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-07-02T20:52:41.000-0400) ===
Please listen to your intuition that the amount and tenor of your visits has become counterproductive. You matter too. I think it’s time for you to inaugurate a new summer schedule! 😎

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-07-02T09:04:08.000-0400) ===
Yes, most definitely you should be scheduling visits with her. No more every day visits. If you want to continue doing her laundry pick it up once a week and drop it off once a week. I would strongly suggest you stop doing her laundry altogether and let the facility do it. She is going to complain about the laundry either way regardless if you're doing it or the LTC staff because it's something to complain about. Save yourself some work and aggravation and just let them take care of it.

You need a break from her. So take one. You've got a lot going on right now and dealing with her complaining and demands is not a priority. If she is safe, clean, fed, and her medications are being taken care of, you can take step back and only visit once or twice a week. You need to take some time and it's okay to include yourself in your own life. 

If she doesn't want to socialize, that's on her not you. Geaton in the comments is right. You're not responsible for her happiness. She has dementia so you will not be able to please her. She may be nice as pie to the staff (which is very common) then turn on the demands, complaining, and orneriness when you come around. So let the staff deal with her while you take care of yourself and the business of selling the house.

You know, your mother may be getting on very well and adjusting to facility life. I was a staff supervisor at an AL. We had residents who were very pleasant, social, and the life of the party. The second one of their grown kids or grandkids called or showed up, it was like flipping a switch. The gloom and doom, misery-spreading, complaining, demands, and orneriness would start. I remember one who would tell her daughter she was starving because the food was so terrible. One day I asked her in front of her daughter and granddaughter why she was on her third plate from the buffet if the food was so bad. The food at the AL was so good. Like a really good restaurant. When family visits or calls, they turn it on.

Don't worry so much about your mother. She will be fine if you cut back on the visiting and give yourself a bit of a break.

=== COMMENT 5 (2026-07-02T07:29:43.000-0400) ===
Expect it. Ignore it, or avoid it. You aren't responsible for her happiness. There is no more "happy" for someone who has dementia no matter how much you bend over backwards for them. You don't have to lose your own happiness or peace. You need to fight to keep it.

If the facility has an Activities Director talk to them about encouraging (or tricking) her into doing more at the facility. You cannot be her Entertainment Committee. You don't have to give her a reason for visiting less -- don't even bring it up, don't mention any change, just do it. Change the subject and keep the calls short. 

My 97-yr old Mom lives next door to me. Sometimes I go an entire day without going over there, just calling to check in. She calls me and obsesses over minutae or things that aren't important and just drains my time and patience. It takes practice. The therapist isn't going to wave a wand and make the difficult emotions go away... you have to practice it and remind yourself that you aren't obligated to orbit around her because it doesn't improve anything and just robs from your daily life. You're on a marathon with her on this journey. It will only get worse so you have to train yourself to ignore certain things. 

You can do it!

My mom has been living with me for nearly four years as her dementia has gradually gotten worse. Last time we went for a drive to the eye doctor and dentist she was worse than I thought: argumentative in the car thinking we were going the wrong way and wanting to “chit chat” at 2 am in the hotel and then not wanting to get up in the morning. Its like pulling teeth even at home to get her to eat once a day. So for the last eight weeks I was going to call about getting her into a nursing home but kept stalling and lately just hiding in my room most of the day, having dinner with her and going to bed. Pretty much not wanting to deal with the situation or the constant questions that drive me nuts or constant asking what to do etc and I have been ambivalent, angry, frustrated and just plain depressed.
Last weekend we had supper Saturday night and Sunday I stayed in bed all day so by Monday night when I get up and go to see her (she sleeps on her sofa in the living room because its comfortable), she had fallen and I didnt know when. Ambulance took her to hospital and she had bruises down both arms and said her back hurt which I have always figured is her pinched nerve in her lower back. Doctor said she was dehydrated, her electrolytes were off, her kidneys were bad and she has a bad UTI and an open wound on her back and infection possibly in it. Even if I had checked on her sooner, I wouldnt have known about the UTI or wound on her back which sounds like a bedsore almost. So I feel bad. As much as I want her to pass before she gets much worse, I certainly didn't and dont want her to suffer. She's on antibiotics and fluids and potassium to get her electrolytes back up. Shes 89 now and looks so tiny in the hospital bed. The nurse talked about getting her into a home when shes better and some rehab for getting her back on her feet again. So my advice for others is dont hesitate to get your loved one into a home where skilled health care can look after them. (I was stalling because I worked in a nursing home back in the 1990s and pretty much learned the best thing is to be able to afford a private nurse to avoid problems with understaffing etc in nursing homes).

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-08-20T18:16:14.000-0400) ===
Dehydration and UTI's are really common in the elderly.

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-08-20T18:02:32.000-0400) ===
You worked in ONE nursing home and decided to paint all of them with the same broad brush from that one experience. I’m truly sorry you and mom both are going through this, but the lesson here is to find the best care you can when your burnout is overwhelming. You chose to avoid, stay in bed, and not act. No reason to wallow in guilt, it’s a useless emotion. Move forward now, doing what it takes to find a good situation for mom. Hospital social workers usually are knowledgeable on this. That’s how we found a good place for my mom and got great help with her admission process. I wish you and mom both healing and peace

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-08-20T15:53:43.000-0400) ===
I'm glad that your mom will now be going into a care facility when she leaves the hospital where she'll receive the 24/7 care she now requires, and where you can get back to just being her loving child and not her overwhelmed and burned out caregiver.
And DO NOT under any circumstances bring her back home when she's done with rehab but insist that she now must stay there.

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-08-20T11:27:40.000-0400) ===
Please, don't blame yourself. Its called burnout and you were trying to deal with it in your way. We all are dehydrated when we go into a hospital. I don't think any of us are hydrated enough. You have no idea when she fell. I have Creatine in my bloodwork, precursor to kidney problems. Not dangerous levels yet but at 76 it probably will get worse. Water only helps 10%. Moms potassium levels were low too, she was 89. The wound, if at the base of her spine, there is no fat there and skin gets paper thin. It may have started as a little red spot and overnight became a sore. That could have been missed in a NH. You can't blame yourself for things that happen as we get old. Our bodies start going.

Time to place her so you can be a daughter and not a caregiver.

=== COMMENT 5 (2026-08-20T11:25:32.000-0400) ===
What a distressing situation. Live-in caregiving can wear you down. I took care of my paralyzed father for several years and when you are 24/7 it can be so difficult and isolating. (And there was no dementia involved and I shared care with a wonderful sibling.) I know from experience that mistakes can happen. 😞

It sounds like you are beyond tired and burned out. This is the kind of scenario many of us here are leery of when family members want to try to be everything to their loved ones for years on end without real help and breaks. Caregiving needs to work for both parties and it sounds like the situation is no longer working. Without guilt I would move forward and find the help you both need, whether in your home or finding another setting for your mom. 

All the best to you and keep us posted. 😊

=== POST ===
My Dad's 78 and I'm 52. Before this I lived on my own for 3 years. I'm very independent and self sufficient. My Dad is selfish, thoughtless and a very big presence. I feel like I've lost my home, my refuge. My Dad can't afford to live independently, so I feel like I've got no choice. I'm wondering if the way I'm feeling is partly because of the shock of the change.

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-09-26T21:02:32.053-0400) ===
Mandala.....people are coming out of the woodwork all of a sudden to create new accounts in order to comment on your post, guilting you and trying to say you don't "love" your father if you don't keep him! That he "sacrificed" for you by having sex one night and getting mom pregnant, when nobody knows the true story! Perhaps these newbies don't realize A.C. is a SUPPORT forum and not a place to kick a hurting person in the gut when they reach out for help, idk. What I do know is that there are many ways to love and support a parent w/o taking them into your home! Please think about all the sensible, unemotional comments you've been given and avoid those which try to make you feel like a Bad Person, ok?

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-09-24T11:15:19.973-0400) ===
Find dad a room to rent elsewhere. That's my suggestion. When do difficult people ever get less difficult? Under what circumstances will you be happy to have this man living with you? Get him out now before he gets comfortable and you have to evict him. Tell him you made a mistake, you were having a hot flash and not thinking clearly. Anything. Take responsibility for it. Then get busy finding him room and board somewhere.

After my divorce in the very early 2000s, I mistakenly took my half brother in because his gf was abusive and his lifestyle was awful. So I moved him to Colo from N.Y. thinking he'd be helpful to me. Ha. He was an anchor around my neck, a slob, did nothing, slept in, and acted like a fool wearing Hulk Hogan clothing and wrestling belts 🙄. When I could stand no more, I called around and found him a room to rent back in his home town in N.Y. and convinced the homeowner to take him, sight unseen, by paying his rent in advance for a few months. I had my brother pack up his stuff in boxes and UPSed them out to his new address, and flew him OUT of the state. Phew. It cost me but it was worth every penny. 

Cut your losses NOW and get dad set up elsewhere, preferably in another city far away. Love ya dad, just can't live with ya.

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-09-24T09:41:56.877-0400) ===
No, it won't get better, but you aren't stuck with it. Many people have made the same mistake, and the good news is that you can get out of it. Read the comments on this site to learn of ways to escape. 

And then never do it again! You're now smarter than that.

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-09-24T20:50:35.267-0400) ===
Mandala, NO, it will not get better! It can only get worse!

PLEASE, make a plan for your dad to live independently - you can help him to apply for senior HUD housing which is government subsidized apartment living for seniors and disabled.
Why on earth did your dad move in with you anyway? What was the discussion beforehand? I'm only asking because if you agreed, or if you thought this was an acceptable idea, then he moved in with an expectation that this was agreeable to you. Maybe you thought it would be, until your personalities clashed. It's hard learning to live with anyone after you've lived on your own for years.
And, yes, the shock of this significant change to your lifestyle is probably taking you by surprise. You thought everything would go on as it has, with this other person in your home and life every day?
It's up to you to decide what you are and are not willing to live with.
Maybe you can have a meeting with Dad and make up some house rules that you both abide by. That could work. Remember, this is a transition for him, too. 

You are not obligated to provide your father a place to live. His decisions and life choices have landed him where he is. I think you would feel better if you help him to find somewhere else to live independently and you can get together as often as you want. If he is unable to live independently, then consider Assisted Living, Memory Care, and Skilled Nursing facilities for him. If he has limited income and assets, help him to apply for Medicaid, which will pay for him to have the services he needs and qualifies for.

=== COMMENT 5 (2026-09-26T14:23:48.450-0400) ===
My 90 year old mother moved in 4 years ago. I thought it was going to be a short stay. It does not get better. It was not part of my life plan. She doesn't think she is a burden, but it's another person I have to wait on, cook for, bring to the store, do her pills and prepare all her meals and listen to her complain . It's now more stressful if I want to go on vacation with my husband. She only uses the microwave but I still worry she will leave something on and cause a fire or something if she gets more forgetful. This is my home and I am delaying retirement because I don't want to be home full time caring for someone who is spoiled and just expects everything is for her benefit.

=== COMMENT 6 (2026-09-24T09:50:06.893-0400) ===
I had a father like that. For now, this man needs you more than you need him. You must make it clear that this is your home and there are rules he must follow to live there. Its no longer father and child, your both adults. Do not enable/disable him. If he can do for himself than you don't do it. My Dad was used to be waited on by my Mom. I would not have done that. He went before Mom so I was left with the easier of the two.

If Dad is just only getting Social Security and maybe a pension, HUD does have apts for people like him. They charge 30% of a persons monthly income. He would be responsible for the electric, phone, cable and personal needs. He can get food stamps at that point. I use Tracfone for my Cell. Its pay as you go or a yearly plan at $125 a year. He can stream and have no cable. There maybe Senior bussing if he needs it. Your County Office of Aging can help you find resources. These places have a waiting list so get his name in now.

=== COMMENT 7 (2026-09-24T14:09:52.263-0400) ===
Don't talk yourself into thinking this is okay, or that you're being unfair, or that it will get better. It won't. 

You aren't responsible for your father's failure to plan for his senior years. As others have said, check with what services are available for low-income seniors, and get him on waiting lists. Start looking now for people renting out rooms or basements in their homes. You can probably sign him up for Meals on Wheels.

How did your dad's circumstances change, that led him to moving in with you? Where was he living before?

=== COMMENT 8 (2026-09-24T14:23:01.053-0400) ===
You have lost lost your home and shouldn't allow Dad more than a few months to find his own place to live! YES, you have a choice. You need to get this fixed quickly.

Why did you think your Dad is your sole responsibility? You have only been on your own 3 years since age 49? Do you have spouse or kids?

Start by letting Dad know this is a temporary setup, so start looking for other low-income places for Dad. Is the problem only "affordability?" Or has Dad been declining medically, not just financially?

=== COMMENT 9 (2026-09-24T09:08:03.510-0400) ===
Your father is 78 years old and low-income. There is special senior housing for people like him that younger people who are the working poor can't get near. His name has to start going on every waiting list for senior housing there is. 

In the meantime, don't tolerate any bad behaviors from your father. Speak very plainly to him so there's no minsunderstanding or misinterpreting anything you say. Maybe even have someone else around to witness this conversation. Or tell your father you are going to record it. This is to keep things simple. 

Make sure he doesn't forget whose house he lives. Remind him os this when you need to and that eviction is always a possibility if he gets too obnoxious or demanding in your home. Be sure he understands that being a senior does not protect him from eviction. Also, that living with you is temporary and only until he gets into senior housing or whatever other type of living situation is going to be for him.

If you've enjoyed living alone, then you have lost your refuge. If you like living alone it's not going to work out with anyone living with you. Even if they are pleasant and helpful. Living alone has it's pros and cons too. 

Help your father get into a living situation that he can afford. Usually senior housing based on a person's income have waiting lists that can be several years long. Many people rent rooms in their houses and that could be a possibility for him. Margaret is right. Give him six months. If the wait is longer for a senior community and likely will be, he will hav to move into a rented room in a private home and wait it out.

=== COMMENT 10 (2026-09-26T14:40:01.393-0400) ===
It will not get better. Your dad's financial situation is not your responsibility.

Mom was diagnosed with COPD years ago however, she doesn’t need meds for it, or oxygen or anything. Her AL charges her $205 for COPD management. I’ve argued that there is nothing to manage but they tell me since she was diagnosed with it they have to manage it. I asked WHAT exactly are you managing?? No answer. === COMMENT 1 (2026-10-17T07:27:12.387-0400) ===
Floridian here. A guy on our street is doing time for Medicare fraud for over charging in his chain of nursing homes. 
He scammed tens of millions of dollars from over billing. 

our state has numbers you can call to report over billing.

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-10-16T17:59:42.260-0400) ===
Does Medicare and Medicaid pay for assistant living facilities

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-10-15T13:32:57.743-0400) ===
FG22, on removing AL from auto pay, I had to do this with my moms IL billing. It required an “in person at the bank w/a bank officer” meeting. Will be a form her bank has attesting that the situation with the vendor is settled. So you have to be a signatory on the account. 

A sticky in all this could be that her AL contract requires written “notice” by her or you as her POA with a fixed exit date in order to wind down her account by choice. It’s something to pay attention to. Not unusual for ILs & ALs charge whatever mo fees EVEN IF resident is in the hospital or in rehab. Please pls read her contract so no surprises. 

On another note….. so in your update yesterday…. mom now hospitalized with sepsis? Sepsis is serious. Most facilities will not allow those w/sepsis.

Yes, a Personal Care Assistant (PCA) can hold a [member], but it is heavily regulated and can present significant legal and ethical challenges.

How this is handled depends entirely on whether the PCA is a professional hire or a family member.

Scenario 1: Professional or Agency-Hired PCAs

If the PCA is a professional hired through an agency or acting as an independent contractor, they generally cannot or should not be the POA. [

Conflict of Interest: Most professional care agencies explicitly forbid employees from accepting fiduciary or legal roles like a POA. It creates a massive conflict of interest where the person providing the care is also managing the money that pays for that care. [1, 2, 3]

Exploitation Risks: Courts and financial institutions closely scrutinize situations where a paid, non-family caregiver is granted a POA. If it looks like undue influence was used to get a vulnerable person to sign over control, the POA can be legally challenged and invalidated. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Scenario 2: Family Members Acting as PCAs

If the PCA is an adult child or relative who is acting as the primary caregiver, it is very common and completely legal for them to hold the POA. 

Personal Care Agreements (PCA Contracts): Often, families will draft a formal contract called a Personal Care Agreement (also abbreviated as a PCA). This contract allows the family caregiver to be paid legally out of the elder’s funds without violating Medicaid look-back rules. [1]

Signing the Agreement: If the care recipient is still mentally competent, they must sign the PCA contract themselves. If they are already incapacitated, a family member who already holds the financial POA may have the authority to sign the contract on their behalf—essentially hiring themselves to be the caregiver. 

Critical Precautions for Caregivers with POA

If you are acting as both the PCA (caregiver) and the POA (legal decision-maker), you must take steps to protect yourself from allegations of financial elder abuse:

Keep Meticulous Records: Log every hour worked, care tasks performed, and keep every single receipt for expenses paid out of the principal's accounts. 

Charge Market Rate: Do not overcharge. The pay rate specified in the Personal Care Agreement must match local averages for professional caregivers. 

Be Transparent: Share the arrangement openly with other family members or siblings to ensure there are no surprises or accusations of hidden asset transfers.

This is when there is general recall of an event, but the details are missing because of memory issues. This causes the PWD to "fill in" the missing information with something that makes sense in the moment— often they will assume the "hero" or "victim" role in any re-telling. Good morning ALZ family!  

It is with heavy heart that we have finally put my Dad to rest after what seemed to be a short battle with VD.  It became very evident to my sisters and I, in May of this year, that he was declining and could no longer be cared for by our mother so he was placed in a facility for "rehab".  From there he declined so fast it was hard to keep up with what was happening.  In our state there are not may facilities that offer help to those patients with aggression caused by the dementia, so he bounced in and out of ER rooms, hospital stays and in his final days, an adult psychiatric ward.  It was a very heartbreaking experience for us all and eye opening to the neglect this disease gets in the medical world we live in here in the United States.  

His diagnosis was missed by several doctors and with HIPPA, if it was caught, no one knew so we could start getting help sooner.  Looking back there were signs of his decline for years, we just didn't see it and if we did, we chocked it up to him being an a**hole.  He was always a sarcastic person and full of colorful words, but in the last few years it became hateful and hard to deal with so my sisters and I chose not to deal.  We missed out on so much time because we didn't know.  My mom dealt with it and hated him most of the time, she was close to divorce right before his diagnosis.  There has to be a better way to get in front of this, it seems like a lot of people chase the disease instead of deal with it upfront.  

I hope that he knew that he was indeed loved, even if the last few years seemed hard and distant from everyone.  My advise to anyone who is seeking help is to make the most of the time you have left, even if you feel overwhelmed, stressed, or angry, because there is always time for that later, but when your loved one is still with you, don't waste your time on the things you cannot control, spend it with the ones you love and making sure they know that they are indeed loved.

The other thing I have learned is communication is key, keep those lines open, make plans together and don't let pride or secrecy stand in your way.  The more your loved ones know the more they can help and when you do leave this world the more they can honor your last wishes.  Never leave them with a pile of unknown to handle, there is so much that happens when a person is gone that they don't need the extra headaches to handle on top of it all.

Thank you for being here for me during this time in my life!  I appreciate what each and every one of you do on a daily basis.  Keep fighting the good fight, it means more than you know to those around you.  Love deep, love hard, and they will forever know.

One of the best ways to manage over-eating, is to remove the visual triggers. If you can keep high calorie treats locked away so she doesn't know about them or "run out" it might be best. Limiting alcohol options will be driven by how much she seeks it out. If she's the type who typically has one glass a night, you might consider only dining at places that don't serve liquor. Some swear by no-alcohol wines but we didn't have success there. We also couldn't water wine beyond about 10% before dad could tell and become aggressive. He was an active alcoholic, so YMMV.

=== COMMENT 6 (2026-10-16T16:20:50+00:00) ===
Dear [member],

I so relate to what you are going through and how much you wish to be able to be different when you feel that anger rising up.  I too have gone through that storm of emotion so many times with my LO.

This may or may not be of help to you but here is what I finally found some understanding and help from.

In Buddhist thought (and this has nothing to do with religion but with a philosophy) we all experience what is called the Two Arrows.  The first arrow is the unavoidable pain that we will all, each and everyone of us, feel because we are human and experience unavoidably painful things in our lives.

The second arrow however, is the additional pain that we inflict on ourselves when we experience the pain of everyday living.

In caregiving the first arrow is the dementia itself.  The endless loops of conversation, the argumentativeness of our LO who's mind is desperately trying to maintain control of itself, the shared loss of memories and the very painful realization, over and over that our LO can no longer use any logic to reason through a situation.  This is the arrow we cannot stop from hitting us  - it just is what it is.

The second arrow though, is the mental anguish, anger and then the self-blame we shoot at ourselves because of the pain of the first arrow. When we get angry at our LO for not remembering or not acting logically, we are essentially demanding and also believing that they control a disease they cannot control. Because they cannot participate in the usual de-escalation processes that partners build with each other or to grasp our reasoning, our anger changes nothing about their behavior. Instead, it spikes our own adrenaline, drains our already depleted energy, and inevitably results in the heavy shame and guilt that follows an angry outburst. The anger is a second arrow because it only harms the caregiver's own nervous system.

We don't have control over the first arrow, but we do have control over  shooting of the second arrow at ourselves.

What I had to do was to try, over and over, to stop shooting that second arrow at myself.  I spent so much time trying to get my LO to remember, to agree with me and to act logically.  Well. . . she just isn't capable of doing that any more - and so I found myself in the endless cycle of trying to be in control and because I literally could not be in control of her dementia I was continually finding myself angry and frustrated with her.  And then I didn't like myself very much.

What I've tried to work on over time (and it does take time and practice) is to accept that my LO's mind is almost always focused on "right now" rather than being able to think logically or strategically.  She really cannot, is not capable of actually focusing on an outcome.  Rather than shoot that second arrow at myself I try, everyday to quit trying to make my LO think logically or rationally. Instead I just try to go along with her frustrating lack of logic, planning and ongoing obsessions.  She just is no longer capable of doing that of thinking logically or rationally. I work on giving up control and try to realize that my job is no longer to "fix" her thinking through things logically or rationally. My job now is to simply manage my own mind and to show up and be present for her.

That doesn't mean I don't ever get angry anymore. I do. But I've also quit trying to view my getting angry as a moral failure on my part.  I try to be compassionate both for my LO's struggle but also for my own struggle which is equally real.  I don't get as angry as often and when I do, I am quicker to realize that it's a signal that my own nervous system is probably at capacity for that moment and maybe I just need to walk away into another room and take a break for myself as well as my LO.  The practice everyday for me is not about never failing, but about recognizing my exhaustion, then forgiving myself for being human, and refusing to shoot that second arrow at myself through a whole lot of self -judgement.  

But I find that if I can keep all of that in mind I am less angry - or at least, I let my anger go a lot faster when I feel it coming on.  And slowly but surely I have found myself to be less and less angry with her.

I don't know if that is helpful at all.  But I appreciate the opportunity to share a portion of my journey with you and I wish you all my best in your own journey and ability to find self-compassion.

Debrah

=== COMMENT 9 (2026-10-19T12:00:54+00:00) ===
@[member] 

Hi and welcome. I am sorry for your reason to be here but pleased you found this place.

You've gotten a lot of good advice here already.

Is this neurologist a specialist in dementia or at a university memory center? Was any bloodwork done to specifically rule out a vitamin or hormone deficiency? Did he have any tests (Pet scan, blood test or spinal tap) to confirm Alzheimer's? Did the neuropsych point to any patterns consistent with Alzheimer's or any other type of dementia? What did "fairly heavy" drinking look like for him in terms of weekly amounts and years? 

It's pretty typical of neurologists to use MCI as a tentative diagnosis and revisit that in 6-12 months. This would especially be true in a situation where there was an addressable condition that mimics dementia. I had this scenario with both my parents. With dad, it was alcohol use. His Thiamine was borderline and he was treated with IV supplementation and told to be abstinent (he was not 100%). He did improve for a time when he couldn't access alcohol, but his new baseline was considerably lower than before. With mom, it turned out she had untreated Lyme Disease— a course of antibiotics and she improved to the point where her MoCA was normal for her age and education. 

Circling back, the alcohol piece could be in play here. My dad did have Wernicke-Korsakoff's Syndrome (WKS) which was caused by alcohol use disorder. There seems to be a genetic piece to this, like AUD it can "run in families". Dad's nephew had WKS from AUD, my younger sister had it in the months before she died from complications of HIV (she wasn't a drinker) and dad had a bunch of elderly aunts and uncles who "were senile" back in the day. One of the tests dad had to confirm his WKS was a specialized PET scan that showed glucose uptake in the brain. Two areas that showed changes for dad were the hippocampus (memory and learning) and the hypothalamus (temp and BP regulation)— these are common in WKS. The twist to dad's story is that he also had Alzheimer's and the symptoms associated with that. Your DH could have both and teasing that out can take time.  

Some things you might see if your DH does have WKS would be— an unsteady gait, eye movements, feeling cold, confabulations (false narratives based on real events) and confusion.

Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome - Wikipedia

Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome: Symptoms, Causes, Treatment

I can appreciate that 6 months seems like forever. That said, being sober in the timeframe and revisiting his cognition and testing in 6-12 months will give a clearer idea of what exactly your DH has going on. 

IME, the best "treatment" for whatever your DH has is to remain sober. He may regain some cognition over time. If it's Alzheimer's, he may be a candidate for infusion therapy that might give him more time (about 8 months on average) in the earlier stages.

IME, "bringing up the tough stuff" can lead to disharmony. 

Many PWD are also impacted by anosognosia which is the inability to fully recognize their deficits. They may cop to a lousy memory, but they may not be able to comprehend just how bad it is nor the other cognitive changes around empathy, apathy, executive function, judgement that also part of the disease. Keep in mind that despite all these losses, emotional intelligence persists will into the latest stages of the disease. The result? A PWD will accurately parse your mood and upset but may not be able to fully understand and process it. 

Given this, dwelling on a PWD's deficits with them and/or the changes in your lives can trigger anxiety and agitation. Most caregivers, whether spouses or adult children, find not engaging their LO in the details or heavy discussions best. I can appreciate wanting to give them a say in decisions that impact them, but sometimes that's not the kindest or safest approach.

The drugs likely shortened his life, but Alzheimer's and vascular dementia are both fatal and there is no upside to living longer in stages 6 and 7 and dying slower.  He didn't appear to be happy and seemed to be suffering greatly. 

I recently got beat up pretty badly on a forum on Facebook for suggesting that a medication adjustment might help with a loved ones behavior problems . The group is for people who have loved ones with dementia. The comments I received were pretty mean suggesting that "drugging" him was wrong. 

It is true drugs can be "chemical restraints", but it is also true that we need to keep people with dementia safe, clean and fed. Sometimes none of those things are possible without medications.

I'll never comment on that forum again.  Don't judge me. Walk a mile in my shoes before you tell me what to do. I did the very best that I could when it came to caring for my DH.

My mom explored this idea with an elder law attorney. The situation might be a bit different— their relationship had been one of highs and lows and had been in a bad place since dad's early symptoms of dementia started almost 10 years prior. She gave up a lot to try to repair the relationship including moving away from the rest of her family and friends.

Mom, like you, didn't feel she could cope with being a caregiver (despite already being one for almost 10 years without realizing it). Dad was a difficult person and mom was angry as one of dad's forms of dementia was alcohol-related.

The way it was explained to us is that a divorce was possible but that costs could be high. Each would need legal representation, dad would also need a guardian ad litem and the court would order neuropsych testing to establish incapacity. This takes time. During the process, dad would need to be cared for; he wasn't safe home alone and wouldn't accept in-home care from anyone but mom.  Their estate would have been split 50/50 and mom might have needed to pay some form of alimony and continue to cover his medical expenses. 

In my county, a divorced spouse loses any say in care decisions and would not be considered for the role of guardian. If there is an adult child or sibling willing, they would be making decisions regarding care, finances and contact with you. If no one else is deemed acceptable, then a professional would be assigned with costs coming out of DH's (and potentially your) funds. 

In the end, mom decided against divorce for a number of reasons. The loss of agency to determine his care stuck in her craw. She still cared deeply and wanted the best for him. As only surviving child, I would likely have been named guardian and mom didn't trust me as we never got along.  The financial piece was a driver as well; dad had already made some financial decisions that cost them at around $400K of their nest egg. She also worried about what others would think and the whole "in sickness and in health" thing. Others were unaware of his past and current behavior, and she didn't want to be judged by them for ditching him when he needed care.

So, she took a gamble and stuck it out. Dad lived another 18 months. Her health suffered during his care but she's older so it's hard to know how big an impact staying had. She did survive with her reputation and a "loving wife" intact (it mattered to her) and the entire estate. TBH, a divorce complicated by dementia in one party probably would have taken at least that long. Had the divorce gone through at 12 months, he'd have had some assets left which would have gone to me and my sister's kids— not mom.

Mom's sister died and we went to Boston for a week for the funeral during which time an old friend kept and eye on dad. Her reports were not good, so we drove home right after the service.
